semantic_correction.stem: A client receiving continuous gastric tube feeding has slid down in bed so the head of the bed is elevated only 10 degrees. There is no contraindication to elevation. Which nursing action best reduces aspiration risk?

options.A: Keep the head of the bed near 10 degrees and reduce the feeding rate, because slower gastric delivery provides adequate aspiration protection while the client remains supine.
options.B: Reposition the client and maintain head-of-bed elevation at about 30 to 45 degrees, while continuing the other prescribed aspiration-prevention and feeding-safety measures.
options.C: Turn the client fully onto one side with the head of the bed flat, because lateral positioning provides equivalent aspiration protection during continuous gastric feeding.
options.D: Pause the feeding whenever the client sleeps and resume it with the head of the bed near 10 degrees, because interrupting nutrition removes the need for semirecumbent positioning.

semantic_correction.rationale: B is correct. The American Association of Critical-Care Nurses Practice Alert on prevention of aspiration in adults lists maintaining head-of-bed elevation at 30 to 45 degrees, unless contraindicated, as an expected aspiration-prevention practice. Current NCBI Bookshelf nursing guidance independently repeats the same recommendation for clients receiving enteral nutrition and identifies low or supine positioning as an aspiration risk. Elevating the head of the bed is one component of a broader aspiration-prevention approach that also includes appropriate tube-placement and gastrointestinal-tolerance assessment. Therefore a client receiving continuous gastric feeding who has slid to approximately 10 degrees should be repositioned to about 30 to 45 degrees when no contraindication exists. A is incorrect because slowing the feeding rate does not substitute for recommended head-of-bed elevation. C is incorrect because flat lateral positioning is not presented as equivalent to semirecumbent positioning for a tube-fed client at aspiration risk. D is incorrect because routine sleep-related feeding interruption with return to near-supine positioning does not replace recommended positioning and may unnecessarily disrupt prescribed nutrition.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests a core aspiration-prevention positioning intervention during continuous gastric tube feeding with one clearly best answer, balanced distractors, current corroboration, and no absolute-word cue.

option_audit.A: Incorrect. Reducing feeding rate does not substitute for recommended head-of-bed elevation in a client who can safely be positioned semirecumbently.
option_audit.B: Correct. Head-of-bed elevation of approximately 30-45 degrees when not contraindicated is an established aspiration-prevention measure during tube feeding.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Flat lateral positioning is not an equivalent replacement for recommended semirecumbent positioning during continuous gastric feeding.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Routine sleep-related feeding interruption and near-supine positioning do not replace head-of-bed elevation and may disrupt prescribed nutrition.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. B directly matches the established positioning recommendation; A substitutes feeding-rate reduction, C substitutes unsupported flat lateral positioning, and D combines unnecessary interruption with continued low elevation.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel bedside positioning/feeding actions of comparable length and specificity; the prior absolute-word distractor was removed and the correct answer is not uniquely detailed by format.
